utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, the Chamber takes this opportunity to inform the parties that it will deliver guidance before the summer recess on how the Chamber expects both of the parties to use court time more efficiently and effectively going forward. Ms. MacGregor, it will be you who will cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Stojanovic will examine you. Mr. Stojanovic - and you find him to your left - is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to tell us for the record, very slowly, your first name and your last name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Zoran Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you at a certain point in time give a statement to the Defence of General Mladic in written form?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have in the e-court document marked 1D01655, that's the 65 ter number. Let me just repeat: 1D01655. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you have in front of you on the screen your statement, and I should like to ask you to see whether these are your personal particulars, the name of the father, the ethnicity, the date of birth; are they correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is your personal signature below these data?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now turn to the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this signature and the date on this page, are they written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, if today I were to ask you the very same questions that we asked you during the proofing for this trial, would you, after having made the solemn declaration today in court, repeat the same answers as the ones that you gave us and that are contained in this written statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender the statement of Witness Zoran Nikolic, which bears the 65 ter number 1D01655, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1655 receives number D581, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, I should like to read a summary of the statement of the Witness Zoran Nikolic. Up to the outbreak of the war, Witness Zoran Nikolic -- up to the outbreak of war in Foca, the witness, Zoran Nikolic, worked in the employment office of the city of Foca. When the war broke out in Foca and the Crisis Staff was set up, TO units were established, which consisted of three platoons organised upon the territorial principle. As the commander of one of the platoons was his brother, Dragan Nikolic, he joined precisely his unit. Already on the 8th of April, 1992, an armed conflict broke out after fire had been opened on Serb territorial units from a modified thrower. The fighting lasted all that day, and in the days that followed, Serbian forces managed to enter the part of the city which is called Aladza and later also the section of the city Donje Polje, where the fighting was the fiercest. In those battles, his brother was killed. The fighting around the city itself lasted for several days. As the Muslims started losing on the battle-field, they started to withdraw from the city, and a large number of Muslim civilians left the territory of the town of Foca together with their armed forces. The reason for their departure was fear because there did not exist any kind of a proclamation order along those lines by the Serb authorities. At that time, there did not exist the VRS in Foca but only Territorial Defence units. In April and May 1992, there was a number of armed groups in the town of Foca, and one cannot say at all whether there existed a single command over those units. At the time when control was assumed over the city of Foca, as far as he understands, there did not exist either a military or political organ that had managed to put under its control all these armed groups. That is a short summary of the witness -- of this witness. And with your permission, I should now like to ask him several questions in connection with his statement. Could we now see in the e-court this document that we now have before us. Let us take a look at paragraph 2 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in paragraph 2 of your statement you stated that during those conflicts you were engaged in the Territorial Defence, and then you say: "And later I was engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska from time to time." Please tell the Court what does this answer of yours mean, to the effect that you were engaged there from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of the conflict, I was engaged -- or better to put it, I joined the unit which was commanded by my brother. And that unit was part of the Territorial Defence. After a month and a half, or more precisely in mid-June, I believe it was the 18th of June, 1992, the Executive Board of Foca municipality instructed me and assigned me to organise the work of an institution, the employment office in Foca. So my engagement on the Territorial Defence started on the 8th of April and ended on the 18th of June. And later after the setting up of the Army of Republika Srpska, I would be engaged as required for the work obligation, if there were some incidents or some situations which so required, during religious holidays as additional security for the lines or when there were some incidents occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in some concrete units at the positions or did you hold some -- did you perform some functions in the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was in the concrete units at the positions. I did not hold any military office, discharge any military function at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement, you speak about the developments on the 8th of April, and you say, if you can see: In the morning we received information -- received notification because there was a connection with the Crisis Staff. My question is: How were you so notified, through what means by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I said, my brother was the commander of this platoon and he was the only one who had a Motorola radio connections, a direct connection to the Crisis Staff. And it was in this way that we received specific orders; and namely, my brother received them and then he relayed them on to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time on the 8th of April in the morning, where was the Crisis Staff? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have that information. And also from earlier, we knew that the Crisis Staff was located in Cerezluk, this is a section of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were the Muslim forces or political forces in Foca, did they have a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were actually right opposite the headquarters of the Muslim Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff of the Muslim organisations of the Territorial Defence. That is how they called their organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment when the tensions ran high between the ethnicities, did you have any information about any negotiations being conducted between the two Crisis Staffs in order to overcome that situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 8th of April, namely, we were informed -- or, rather, we were ordered by the Crisis Staff that on no account should we, without orders from the Crisis Staff, open any fire because in the building of the municipal assembly, at that moment - namely, from 8.00 and on - representatives of the two Crisis Staffs, the Muslim and the Serb, one -- were sitting and talking about the current situation prevailing in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we see in e-court document 1D4511. 1D4511. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the heading of this document states that it was compiled --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please scroll down so that we could see the top left corner and the date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It reads that this is an agreement, and it is indicated it was in Foca on the 8th of April, 1992, and that there are given specific conclusions. And in brackets it is indicated either "Crisis Staffs" or some other organ next to the actual conclusions. Can you tell us what this is about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document is something I saw in the original. I know what it is about, and this is actually the outcome of the talks conducted between the representatives of the Crisis Staffs on that day, the 8th of April, at that time that I just referred to a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to item 10 of this agreement which says: [As read] "The removal of all armed people from outside (crisis staffs) and verification by observers." So I should like to ask you: Was it the case that already on the 8th of April, 1992, there were armed men in Foca who had come from elsewhere, from parts outside the municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Foca, both sides - and I am referring to the Muslims and the Serbs and their organisations on which they worked - and they both sought to organise themselves as best as possible. They all had people from outside. This was not a large number, but it is a fact that they were present there on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they precisely the people that you referred to in the two last paragraphs of your statement when you said that you don't know under whose control they were or that they were under anybody's control?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a lesser number of people. After the beginning of the conflict, some five or seven days later, this number of people who had come from other parts increased. I meant for the most part those people, but more than that I was referring to the groups that arrived during or after the end of the fighting in the city proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were those armed groups from, if you know? Or where did they come from to the area of Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Serbia, Montenegro, Sandzak, possibly from some other areas too. But mostly from Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the document 65 ter 1D4511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to see the bottom of the page. Witness, you said that you saw the original of this document. Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I saw the original of this document. There were several signatories. As for this that you've shown me, I recognise only one signature, and others can only be discerned slightly. There were several signatories. Do I need to add anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to know the names of the people you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do recall, because it was an interesting event, noteworthy. On that day in the building of the municipality, in the office of the president of the municipal assembly, the following persons were present: Radojica Mladjenovic, president of the Executive Board; Taib Lojo, president of the municipal assembly; whereas Edhem Varajic [phoen], who was appointed chief of the military department after the democratic changes. Then as far as I can remember, there was Vojo Bodiroga, he was a member of the Executive Board; then Predrag Lakic, also a member of the Executive Board. And Aganovic was there, too, but I cannot recall his first name. He was a member of the Executive Board as well. All of them were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The testimony so far about this document and about this witness's knowledge about the agreement goes beyond the scope of the statement. And in the agreement that we'd put to the Defence, because this witness was appearing in violation of the agreement we made, was that his testimony on direct would be narrowly within the scope of the direct. I'm not objecting at this point, but the Prosecution hasn't had an opportunity to prepare for this topic of cross-examination -- for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, any reason why you went beyond the scope of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just put a question that corresponds to the statement, paragraph 10 of the statement. I did not ask about the signatures and that is not something I asked the witness during proofing. This is an answer to a question put by His Honour Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My objection actually is -- is before the question put by Judge Fluegge. It has to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be -- Mr. Stojanovic, where is there any reference to such an agreement in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no mention of the agreement, Your Honour. Paramilitary forces, conditionally speaking, armed groups that weren't under anybody's control. So I found a link in paragraph 10 of this agreement that supports part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is nothing about an agreement in paragraph 10, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This is the agreement. And in paragraph 10 there is a reference to armed persons who should be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is no objection at this moment. But to say that this is clearly set out in the statement, there is no way of that, Mr. Stojanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think we first need a number. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Stojanovic, I just want -- this document doesn't tell us who are the parties to the agreement, and this is an agreement that this Court can't take cognizance of when we don't know who are the parties to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no problem with asking this. We did notify the Prosecution on time that we would be using this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document will speak for itself on that point. It's not the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4511 receives number D582, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, is there an objection against admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D582 is admitted into evidence, Mr. Stojanovic, but the objection was about notice. And there is certainly some merit in it. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to have an answer from the witness. I asked him who signed the statement. Then you, Mr. Witness, you answered who was present. You listed quite a lot of people present in the office when this agreement was signed. Did all these people sign this, the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I said a moment ago. I mentioned all of the persons who were present. And I do apologise that I did not mentioned Josip Milincic. All of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not my question. Did all these people sign the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way to have the original sooner or later available? I mean the original not cut off at the bottom but -- Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the information I have, this is in the Prosecution collection; whereas we managed to find this document while we were preparing through EDS. So this was disclosed to us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm informed by Ms. Stewart that this is the best copy that the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we have to do with it for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Actually, Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to ask that we go back to the witness's statement, D581, if I remember correctly, if I noted it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm waiting for it to see -- this document. Mr. Stojanovic, there is not a word not only about an agreement but there is also not a word about this witness being present at the meeting where this agreement, apparently, was signed. So therefore, there is really a notice problem because the Prosecution might have prepared for to search for such a meeting and who were present, et cetera, and with this statement they're unable to do so. Please proceed for the time being, but it's not how it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at paragraph 7 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Nikolic, this is what you say in paragraph 7. At one point in time fire was opened at a police vehicle and that was after a modified launcher had been used against you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, first, what kind of motivated launcher this, the one that fired at you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that you did not formulate this properly. This is not what I had stated. In my statement I said, and this is what I wrote, that fire was opened before the reaction of the modified launcher. On our right-hand side there were territorials. Our platoon consisted of chosen people irrespective of their territory. This was an elite unit, a select unit. I cannot say exactly now which side opened fire first. It seemed to me that it was at the same time. And the reason for opening fire was the arrival of the police vehicle and its movement towards the building of Focatrans where the Crisis Staff of the Muslims was. We had strict orders not to open fire. When arriving in that territory, my brother took over command over these territorials as well, so he immediately ordered a cessation of all fire. This was communicated and fire from our side stopped because we strictly abided by the order; namely, that without any order of the Crisis Staff we should not open fire. That is what this is all about. So could you please repeat the second part of your question to me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of modified launcher was this, the one that fired at you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the time I did not know what that was. I could not recognise the weapon they used to fire at us, but later on I found out -- actually, I saw this device, this modified launcher. This was actually a launcher, a rocket launcher adapted for the use of shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic. Witness, you said that you did not state what was read to you. You said in your statement you said that fire was opened before the reaction of the modified launcher. The statement, however, reads that only after the modified launcher was used against you that fire was opened. So that's something different from what your testimony is now. If there is any translation issue, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber would like to be informed about it. But I just put it to you that what you now say is not what we read in your statement. Is the statement wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm afraid that what I'm -- what I said in the statement is being misinterpreted. So where I was, where I was involved in the platoon that was commanded by my brother, and he also took over command over another unit, the order was not to open fire. However, what happened was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I stop you there. I'll read the relevant part of the statement. "Fire was opened only after a modified launcher was used against us, and we responded by opening fire," et cetera. Now you said here in court that you may have been misunderstood and you said fire was opened before the reaction of the modified launcher. Now, that's not the same. Therefore, instead of further explaining, what is wrong: What we read in the statement or what you said in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, you read out the other part or, rather, the second sentence. Please allow me to read the sentence that precedes the sentence that you read out. "Fire was opened at a police vehicle, and I later learned that Abid Ramovic was killed at that time and that another police officer was wounded in that vehicle. Fire was opened only after that modified launcher was used against us when we responded by opening fire on the Focatrans buildings and the facilities immediately above Focatrans from which fire was opened." So what I'm trying to say is that irrespective of the order, I think that the unit next to us reacted and the Muslims fired as well at the police vehicle. So after a while, on orders from my brother, who was the commander of that unit, fire was stopped and the situation calmed down. Immediately after that, half an hour later, this modified launcher started firing. Then my brother established contact with the Crisis Staff. I was right there next to him. He explained the situation, that we are under heavy fire, and then he received orders to respond. So that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stojanovic, next time take care that the statement reflects what the witness intends to say because what he actually now is telling us, that fire was opened, that later a modified launcher was used, and that after that again fire started. Which is not what the statement says. It says "only after." But we now understand the testimony better, and we still do not understand why the statement is phrased as it was. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was your impression about the weaponry and the power of the weaponry of the opposing side at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise in putting your question? Do you mean at that moment, what my impression was then, at that moment that I spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment of the fighting between the 8th and of the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Believe me, at first I did not expect or assume that they could fire at us with such weaponry and such force. As for the actual area where we were, this kind of force was used and at -- and we could not have believed what was happening. It was terrifying. On the other hand, our unit and the units of the Territorial Defence were armed with light weapons, rough rifles, M48 for the most part. The only automatic weapon, an automatic rifle, was the one that my brother had. And also there were two semiautomatic rifles that were in the hands of some soldiers. All the others had M48 rifles and used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D2704.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document of the Supreme Command staff of the security administration of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, bearing the date 17th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now please see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The title of this report of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is: "Some intelligence on the causes of the lack of organisation in the defence of Foca against the conquest by the aggressor and the persecution and plight of the majority Muslim population." Please look at the last paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is, Your Honours, the beginning of the second paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where it is stated in this report after the democratic elections for -- Lojo Taib was an electrical engineer, a respectable citizen, was appointed vice-president -- was appointed president of the Foca SO. However, from the very beginning, Senad Sahinpasic, aka Saja, and Halid Cengic, who are related, having the greatest political influence in the SDA thanks to the powerful support of influential relatives and friends from Sarajevo, especially Muhamed Cengic, the then deputy prime minister -- minister. Is this information consistent with what you know about the people who were in the government, in the municipality of Foca at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know where from this man who submitted this report or this memo drew his information. It is as if he had asked me. It is everything that I knew about the organising of the Muslims. The reference to these names and their activities in the area of the municipality of Foca is consistent with what I know, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just move to the next page in B/C/S and in the English version it is this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you meanwhile inform us, Mr. Stojanovic, where we find anything about your present line of questioning in the statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, this part of my question referred to just the political struggle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the situation with the weapons in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly my problem, that it is about something different from what is found in the witness's statement. And then to explain that it is different is not a proper answer to my observation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last sentence in the first paragraph here where it is stated they included Aziz Sljivo and a wide circle of men loyal to them in the arms smuggling so that the Muslim people in this area, for fear of the ever-increasing Chetnik threat, are giving the last penny to those whom they have elected to protect their interests, to supply them with weapons. So they paid the rifles that Sahinpasic and Cengic are selling them, 1.200 to 1.500 German marks. According to some intelligence, 5.200 rifles came to Foca via the SDA which Sahinpasic and Cengic sold. My question is: Did you know about this or anything similar about the arming of the Muslim population in Foca municipality at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have such information from a number of sources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, you can probably guess my objection is still about notice. Specifically right now, he's being asked about his knowledge about the arming of the Muslims. This is not something that was covered in depth. And I did have notice of this document, but would not have been able to foresee this as a line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, where do we find it in the statement and where do we find it in the Rule 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it does not contain this part. It does not arise from the statement given to the witness, except for what he said today in relation to arming and the amount of equipment at the -- the adversary side had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you please put questions to the witness which are in direct relation with his statement and are covered by the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have something to say. Mr. Stojanovic, I've got also another problem of a different kind. You tell the witness a story and then telling him how arms were acquired and paid for with German marks, and then having told him that story, you ask him if he knows anything about it. Why do you lead and not ask questions? Why do you tell him a story before you ask him a question? That's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I showed him the document. I did not ask him that. That is what the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, this is what you read. Do you want me to read what you said to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But look at what you said before you put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a quotation from a document of the Army of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The proper way would be, Mr. Stojanovic, to ask the witness whether he has any knowledge about arming, then ask him what he knows about it, and if there is any reason then to compare that with any document, you put that document to him. But you do not start reading the document saying, "So they paid the rifles," et cetera, according to it challenges this and this and this, and then to ask the witness: "My question is: Did you know about this or anything similar ..." You've given the whole story before you ask him whether he has any knowledge about. It should be the other way around. And I invited you to put questions to the witness which are -- can be directly linked to his statement and are covered by the Rule 65 ter summary, and please limit yourself to that. Apart from that your time is over already by far because you claimed half an hour. You started at 20 minutes to 10.00. It's now close to 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be concluding, Your Honours, I just have another question. One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Nikolic, you say that a large number of Muslims left Foca that night. Will you tell Their Honours where did the Muslim population and armed members of the Muslim people head for when leaving Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Several days later, after several days of fighting in the city, when Bosniak - i.e., Muslim forces - at that time realised that they were losing on the battle-field, first their political and military leaderships, in the night of the 12th, as far as I know, they were the first to leave. Then the military forces became panic stricken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you there. The question was where did they go. Not why did they go, not who went. Where did they go as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that most of the Muslims, armed persons and inhabitants, left in the direction of Ustikolina and further on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the last word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last word you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your last question, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was, Your Honours. And I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it would be an appropriate time to take a break first. Could you give us a further estimate, Ms. MacGregor, on how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Last night we informed the parties that we expected an hour and a half and I hope to go under that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break first. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. We resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber wonders what will be the consequences. Are there any changes to your witness list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we had Mr. Simovic as the next one, and then -- but he will appear, will he not appear today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is not our plan to bring Mr. Simovic today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just spoke with Mr. Ivetic. The -- we are trying to accommodate Witness and Victim Unit. At the beginning we had witnesses here for a long time, so we were criticised heavily by this unit who is really helping agree time to everybody. And we organised our witnesses coming here based on the estimate received from the Prosecution. As we saw lately there were some cuts in cross-examination and that created a shortage, we can say, of witnesses on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now do we have another witness then for later today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic is the only one who -- whom -- who was spoken to, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I'm not sure that he is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the day before yesterday, but Mr. Ivetic was in the courtroom yesterday, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then you have to organise it in such a way that -- but let's first continue with this witness. But please reconsider whether or not Mr. Simovic would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I know we will change the way we bring witnesses here. We will have to add extra day, so I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we have to reason that to Victim and Witness Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We hope that they will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for today, please consider whether or not - and we would urge you - to call Mr. Simovic as the next witness to start today. Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready -- no, apologies. Ms. MacGregor, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Nikolic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. MacGregor. You'll find her to your right. Ms. MacGregor is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. This is the first time that you testified at this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, it is correct. This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And this is also the first case for which you've given a written statement at this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic showed you your statement earlier on the screen, and you agreed that you signed it on June 8th, 2014. Can you just tell us where it was that you signed your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Other than members of the Mladic Defence team, were there any other people present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. There were other witnesses waiting outside, but in the actual room in which I signed the statement, there were only the Defence team members present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the room outside, did you spend some time waiting along with the other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I was late. Actually, I did not arrive at the scheduled time because I had other obligations so that in the meantime, during the break between my previous obligation, when I came, almost everybody else had already finished, and they were all sitting in this room and talking among themselves. I don't know what about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of those witnesses that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, Petkovic. We call him Miso. I'm not quite sure about his first name. We call him Miso. That's Petkovic. Then I saw, I believe, Trifkovic. I don't know his first name. I didn't pay much attention. I was in a hurry. I was not really interested, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you see a witness with the last name Simovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall having noticed him. I know who he is. I don't think he was present. I'm not sure. I cannot give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the subject matter of your statement. I'm going to take us to April 1992. At that point you were living in Foca municipality you've testified and you said in your statement. Before the war, were you politically active in Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please, could you be more precise? In what sense do you mean "politically active"? I am politically active in accordance with my own needs. If you mean specifically whether I was a member of a political party, the answer is yes. I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you a member of any sort of political assembly or political group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. If I leave aside the League of Communists, I was not a member of any assembly. I was a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And during the war, did your political activity change in its nature in any way other than what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the war? No. But after the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Briefly, can you describe how it changed after the war? What you went on to do that was different than your political activity before the war.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After the war, or more specifically in 1996, in the second half of 1996, I agreed to be involved in a political party that is called the Serb Radical Party. I was nominated by the leadership of that party to be commissioner, to try to establish a committee of the Serb Radical Party in Foca, which I managed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Now, in April 1992, there was a call for mobilisation. Now, were you yourself mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not receive any call-up papers for mobilisation. It is of my own free will that I joined the unit that was commanded by my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: According to your statement, that unit was commanded by a man with or a person with the last name Mandic. What is the first name of that person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in my statement here I did not mention the name of any Mandic. If you can, please show me the statement and let me take a look. But as far as I can remember ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can ask the court officer to please show Exhibit D581, and we'll focus on paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to bring that up for you. While I'm bringing it up, I'm going to direct you to the third paragraph and to the first two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: For the record, I'll read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: But you can also look at it in front of you. "At the beginning of the conflict in Foca I was not a member of any formation. After the Crisis Staff was established in Foca, a unit commanded by Mandic was established." Do you see the sentences I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, in the English Prosecutor it says "Mandic." In the Serbian statement, the one that I signed, that is not what is written. I never mentioned the surname Mandic. I don't know how come you have such a document in the English language, but look at the Serbian version and you will see that there is no such name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I see what you're saying to the extent that I can read it, and I will follow-up with the Defence who provided this translation. Thank you. Moving on to the unit that your brother commanded. Do you know who he was responsible for reporting to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know and at the moments when I was present, he directly reported to the Crisis Staff. I remember that the names were coded or, rather, I remember that Soko was the name via radio communication. They did not actually use real names, so conversations were coded. Therefore, I don't know. If you're asking me about the first and last name of a person who communicated with my brother, I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Although you weren't mobilised, you stated you were an escort of your brother's unit. Can you describe what that role was, what you were responsible for doing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I did not have specific assignments. In the statement I said that I left the town of Foca on the 7th in the evening, after 7.00 p.m., to be specific, when my brother closed the cafe that he owned, and I left Foca together with him. I did not have any specific assignments at that moment. I was present throughout. I was with him throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not have a weapon. However, my brother's brother-in-law had a hunting carbine, 7.62, with optical sights, and he gave it to me so that I would have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the moment when we arrived at the position where we were supposed to be deployed, in a house in the area where the unit was deployed. In this house we found Mitar Filipovic, who is the brother of my brother's wife. He gave me that weapon because he didn't have any others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: According to your statement, there was a list of members of your brother's unit. Now, you -- you saw that list?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My brother said to me that there is a list, and I asked how, in which way, they selected these persons. I talked to him about that, and he said something to me that I found interesting; namely that in that unit, it could not happen that two brothers would be members of that single unit. So this was an unwritten rule. That is how I know that this unit, as he said to me, had about 120 members.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, during Mr. Stojanovic's questions, you also described the unit as "select" and "elite." What did you mean by that? What was your understanding of the role of that unit and why they were selected?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know why they were selected. Since I did not take part in the selection of these people, I don't know how this was done exactly. I just told you about some of the details that I know of. I know, though, that this unit consisted of healthy, young, physically and mentally capable men. So if there were to be some situations that could crop up in the town of Foca at the time, they could act in terms of preventing incidents from happening. In practice, this was an intervention unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The rule you just talked about where two brothers wouldn't be in the same unit, to your knowledge is that a rule that was in place throughout the Territorial Defence or was that a -- was that the only time you heard of that rule as it applied to this specific unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I spoke specifically about the unit that was commanded by my brother. So that rule was not applied to other units that were within the Territorial Defence, as far as I knew and heard. I was only speaking about this particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The other members of your unit, did they -- or of this unit, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can you describe what kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Most of these soldiers had M48 rifles, and that's what they used. A few of them had semiautomatic rifles. And my brother had an automatic rifle with an extended rifle-butt, a wooden rifle-butt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And do you know where your brother's unit received their arms from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My brother and a few other men were involved in the organisation in terms of supplying weapons. I don't know specifically because, in a way, this was a secret. I don't have any information. He never told me how and in which way they obtained some of their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you aware of another intervention unit commanded by Gojko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that moment, in the beginning of the conflict, I did not know that there was a unit that was commanded by Gojko Jankovic. Later on, I found out that in the territory of the local commune and the local communes that gravitate towards his local commune, a group was established and Gojko Jankovic commanded that formation or, rather, that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You just referred to the territory of the local commune and other local communes that gravitated towards them. Can you -- can you just explain to me what you're meaning when you talk about different communes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the municipality of Foca has several organisational sections or, rather, local communes. I don't know the exact number but it was between 20 and 30, closer to 30 than 20. This was a large territory. I think that in terms of the area it encompassed it was the second largest in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Specifically, the local commune of Gojko Jankovic was Brod, and then there was Mjesaja. I cannot say exactly what the territorial organisation was, what all the local communes were. But all of that gravitated towards his local commune. And that goes for the people from that territory as well. So all of these people were involved -- I mean, they came from the neighbourhood, possibly there could have been some people from other territories but this would have been an individual case only.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you personally knew Gojko Jankovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, I knew him for ten years before the war. I am quite sure it's even more than that, but I can say with certainty that it was ten years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When did you learn about his -- that he had established a unit -- or that a unit was established under him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when this happened, but I know at one moment -- or, rather, when I was present during a specific situation, I saw Mr. Jankovic and his unit in a concrete situation when an incident occurred. Or rather, when the armed forces of the Muslims attacked the defence line of the front and when they took our positions. Then, in addition to other units that were involved in order to have these territories recaptured, Gojko Jankovic's unit took part as well. That's when I saw the structure and number of persons involved in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On Saint Nicholas Day 1992. Specifically, the position where I saw him is that of the repeater.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, Major Pejovic, who was a cousin of my wife, so I knew him personally, he was the commander of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska in the area of Foca; or, rather, he stood in for Marko Kovac who was absent at the time. He asked me to be at the command together with him because of a special situation that he happened to be in. At that time, after that situation was resolved and after additional forces - i.e., reserve forces were mobilised, the reserve that existed in Foca - I participated in an action to recapture our positions; i.e., occupy the positions that had been seized by the Muslim Bosniak forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I want to just break this down a bit. You referred to a special situation that he -- that Major Pejovic was in and that because of that, he asked you to be there present at the command. So starting first, what was the special situation that you are describing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejovic called me because he thought that his personal security was threatened at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And then why would he call you specifically to help with that situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He's a human being and a human being always relies on friends when the situations are difficult. He considered me a friend, I consider him a friend, and we were actually kin. And I felt secure when I was in his presence, and he also. And I felt that he would feel secure when I was present during that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: To be sure that I'm understanding you, was he asking you to provide physical security for him in the way that a body-guard or something like that would? That's how I'm understanding what you're testifying about, but if I'm incorrect please let me know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In a sense, you are right. One of the reasons was that practically I should provide physical security for him. But I think that at that time he needed someone also in the psychological sense because he had found himself in a very difficult and stressful situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Returning to Gojko Jankovic's unit. Did that unit report to Major Pejovic or Major Kovac -- excuse me, Mr. Kovac when he was back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at that time Gojko Jankovic's unit was part of the system. It was a part of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Reporting to Colonel Kovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And I apologise for my ignorance, but my understanding is that Saint Nicholas Day is around May 25th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. It is the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was way off. And that would have been Saint Nicholas Day 1992, so December 1992 - thank you - is that right? I see you nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you see Gojko Jankovic in Foca from the start of the conflict throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The first time you saw him was in December 1992 after the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I please have -- excuse me, 65 ter 30985.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I'll tell you about this document. It's from 1993. It's from the Foca Tactical Group to Vojislav Seselj. And if we look at the heading on the left side of the page, you can see Gojko Jankovic is named. Do you see there where it says: "Proposal that Gojko Jankovic be proclaimed Vojvoda" or "military leader." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we look, I'm going to look at the first -- well, the second paragraph under the word "explanation." I'm looking at the end of that paragraph, and I'll read from there. "Jankovic himself formed a special detachment with which he obtained excellent results in the liberation of Foca, Cajnice, and other areas, impressing on his soldiers and his fellow commanders by example how to fight against the Ustashas for our Serbian people." Is this description of Jankovic's activities during the war consistent with what you know about him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment on this. I never had occasion to make a profile or to make any kind of structure associated with the person of Gojko Jankovic; therefore I would not venture, pursuant to this or on the basis of what is available, to give any comment or any opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution moves to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30985 receives number P6683, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you aware that -- of another unit commanded by Dragoljub Kunarac that was in Foca during 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you personally know Kunarac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you also at this time know a man named Pero Elez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not for a certain period. Actually, I knew the late Pero Elez since I was nine years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And he commanded a unit as well in Foca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you know a man name Predrag Trivun?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did he also command a unit in Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In 1992 did you see Kunarac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Kunarac only on one occasion, just like Mr. Jankovic whom I also had occasion to see on just one occasion but a different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What was the occasion when you saw Mr. Kunarac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that it was in 1993 when an attack had been organised against Gorazde. I was on the right bank of the Drina river. And at that time he was assigned to bring us to a specific destination, to a specific spot, within our work obligation. He was practically our guide, and that spot where he took us was contaminated by infantry mines, and he did that successfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have a few questions about the -- specifically about the night and the next day of the take-over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, let me ask one question for clarification. Mr. Nikolic, you said -- you mentioned two persons, Mr. Kunarac and Mr. Trivun, and you said they were commanders of units. To which army did these units belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the outset of the conflict, they were members of the Territorial Defence. And afterwards, I believe in the beginning of July, they became part of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that on the evening of April 8th -- or on April 8th, when you were positioned across from the Focatrans building, that a man named Abid Ramovic was killed. This is in your statement at paragraph 6. Was he a Muslim fighter? If you can just answer out loud for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the time when he was killed, he was a policeman. He was not a fighter because he simply didn't have the time for that. So he was killed on the 8th of April in his vehicle -- in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And he was Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This was a mixed patrol. There was one Muslim and one Serb -- there were one Muslim and one Serb in the vehicle. The Muslim, Abid Ramovic, was killed and the Serb was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Moving on to the next day, by this point your unit had progressed into the Aladza neighbourhood. You mentioned in your statement that on that day Rodoljub Trifkovic was killed. Was he a member your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with what you said that was on the next day that we had progressed into the Aladza neighbourhood, whereas it is correct that Rodoljub Trifkovic was a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter said: "I do not agree with what you said that it was on the next day."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to the first paragraph -- excuse me, the sentence of paragraph 9, but I don't think it's essential so I'm going to move on from which day it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now after your brother was killed, did you immediately leave the front lines to return to Prevrac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is a bit difficult for me to actually evoke that particular moment. At the moment my brother was killed, it was my task to protect him and to cover with fire the positions from which the Bosniaks, the Muslims, were opening fire. I apologise for the term I'm using, "Bosniaks," but at that time they were Muslims at any rate. So he crossed the street. This is an alley, a very short and narrow street. And he entered a garden or an area or he went through the gate, better to put it, and I never saw him after that. His cousin was with him, namely, his wife's brother. Some ten minutes later from that -- Mitar emerged from that yard and he informed me that my brother was killed. At that moment I was totally numb, I had no feelings, but all the strength was drained from me and I just collapsed and I needed several minutes to come to. Then together with Mitar, I entered the yard and in this yard there was an old Muslim house, and we reached a small window from which I could see the body of my brother. At that moment I didn't know whether he was alive or dead, so I asked a person or persons -- or the persons who had killed my brother to let me approach my brother to see whether he was alive or dead and to help him, if possible, but there was no reply. A young man, who was a member of this unit and his surname is also Filipovic, he lost it, and he wanted to get inside the room. But when he entered the room, a bullet was heard and he was wounded so that he couldn't actually help me implement my intention. He couldn't do it either. So afraid that I might make a similar try, a similar move, Mitar Filipovic threw a tear gas bomb inside. After that, I tried to enter the room, but the concentration of the gas was so high that it actually stopped me in my tracks and prevented me from physically moving altogether. My friends and fellow combatants took me away from the scene, not far away from it, and I don't know how they managed to pull out my brother's body. A vehicle came, pulled him out -- or actually, transferred him to the field hospital which was 3 kilometres away, specifically in Velecevo, and my fellow combatants -- or one man, Krnojelac, Dragan, actually took me under my arm and took me to a spot where they put me in a vehicle and they drove me to the village of Prevrac, where my wife and children were. At that time we organised for my parents to be transported, and on the following day, because we were unable to bury my brother at the city cemetery, we buried him in the village of Prevrac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam MacGregor, I see that the witness gave about a page of the answer, and in all that page he doesn't say a word about the question you put to him. Your question was: "After your brother was killed, did you immediately leave for Prevrac?"

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I understand the end of his answer to be an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Come again? You understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That the end of his answer was the answer to my question, that he was driven in a vehicle immediately after that to the village of Prevrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought your question was whether this witness went to Prevrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I understand his testimony at lines -- it's page 39, from 7 until 14, specifically 9 and 10: "... Krnojelac, Dragan, took me under my arm and took me to a spot ... they drove me to a village ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If that was the answer, then that would have been the answer. Not the rest of the page that we heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek verification of one thing. You talked about your fellow combatants and you said: "One man, Colonel," and could you repeat his family name. His first name being Dragan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's, I think what I heard before, where the transcript gives a name different from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's wrong again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You read to him Jehovac and where I understand the witness to say "Krnojelac." Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even now, it is -- could you please spell that name --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K-r-n-o-j-e-l-a-c, Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the village of Prevrac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You see, it was the day of the funeral -- or, rather, the day before the funeral. That was the 11th. So then the following day when the funeral took place, and then according to our Orthodox custom there is a certain protocol, if I can put it that way, when, after how many days, a grave is visited and candles are lit. I cannot recall exactly. I wasn't counting the days, but I think that it was seven days, namely, that I stayed in Prevrac for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And after --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And I also went to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. As Judge Moloto has pointed out, we're unfortunately short on time, so if -- if you can just tailor your answer specifically to the questions I'm asking. Although, I know this is a difficult topic. Where did you go after the time that you spent in Prevrac surrounding your brother's funeral? Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My parents lived 10 kilometres away from Foca in a weekend cottage. They had an organised household. They had livestock. And I took care of my wife and children, but I also took care of my parents. I went to see them all the time and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that where you went next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that I did not understand your question. You mean the first time I went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was where did you go after the time that you spent in Prevrac surrounding your brother's funeral. Where did you go next? And I asked whether it was to this weekend cottage that you went. If not, please tell us where you went.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that period, I think that it is about seven days, I took care of my family. I managed to get them out just before the war broke out, a few days, to stay with my brother's father-in-law, Todorovic, and my family were there and -- well, conditionally speaking, maybe it's a harsh word, after the liberation of Foca I returned them to the apartment. Whereas my parents lived in the village of Kuta, 10 kilometres away from Foca. Then I went to see them regularly because they were in great stress, their psychological condition was very grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that these were difficult times, but do I understand that from Prevrac, after this period of seven days, you went to your parents or to that cottage? Because that was the question. And I do understand that it reminds you of unpleasant days, but -- to say the least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try to be as precise as possible. The fact is that my family, that is to say, my wife and two children then, were in the house of Todor Filipovic. Seven days later, I transferred my family and together with them I entered my apartment. Now, from that apartment I regularly went to see my parents who were 10 kilometres away from Foca. I really cannot be anymore precise than this, with the best of wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor will put her next question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just ask, where was your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apartment was in the local commune of Gornje Polje I. The building was 125. It was in the street of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Around June 18th you were ordered by the Municipal Executive Committee to start working at the employment office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Is this the same employment office that you worked at before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What was your role there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was the supervisor. I was the head of the bureau.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you work --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do apologise. My role was to organise the work of the bureau and to provide services to unemployed persons. Because the order of the civilian authorities was to normalise life in Foca as much as possible. That meant having all public institutions function and all institutions that were founded by the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the context is not something Ms. MacGregor might be interested in at this moment, and you explained your role. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you work at the employment offices as a full-time worker?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And from June 18th, 1992, when did you -- till when did you remain in that role?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise on that? Or repeat the question, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that job?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I stayed in that job until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You continue to be employed there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that it's break time and this would be a good time. I have only a few subjects after the break to cover with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break first. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if I understood you correctly. Is your ruling that we bring the next witness even if he's not fully prepared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you first further explain. We had an early finish yesterday. Why -- well, let's say, six, seven, eight hours would not be enough to prepare the witness for appearing as a witness today, where part of this morning was available as well. So all together working time anything between seven and ten hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that I know my colleague Ivetic met with the witness yesterday afternoon, and he is or he was with the witness this morning as well. I'm -- I don't know. Even if he finished his preparations. I'm only asking you is it your ruling that we bring the witness no matter what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll further discuss it, having heard your explanation now. So therefore within the next 20 minutes we'll tell you -- after these 20 minutes, we'll tell you whether the Chamber expects you to call your next witness. Or whatever other matters we would decide. We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you get information from Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then hear that after the break and we'll consider the present situation. We resume at 10 minutes past -- no, let's say 15 minutes past midday. That's a little bit more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I will give you an opportunity to further explain your position. However, I would like already to briefly mention that the 92 ter statement is relatively short and covers quite some matters which were dealt with in -- with the witnesses we've heard the past days, that we already received the corrections to the statement which suggests to us that you do that once you have briefed the witness and once you have gone through this very short statement. And we also noticed that at least considerable time has been available yesterday afternoon and this morning, and therefore the Chamber thinks that you should have very good reasons not to call the witness. But we give you an opportunity to explain your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow us, since Mr. Ivetic was with the witness and he's now with us, so I think it's the best way to allow Mr. Ivetic to explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The clarifications to the statement were sent at approximately 10.38 this morning because at 10.30 I received word that we should end the proofing with the witness, that he should be returned to the hotel to rest, if, indeed, he had to testify today. Per the VWS instructions, the witness should have adequate time to rest between proofing and testimony. The proofing was not done at the time that the clarifications were sent. We were scheduled for proofing from 9.00 to 12.00 this morning. Yesterday, I had a brief opportunity to meet with the witness, who although it is a short statement, this is a witness who has never testified before, either in proceedings at any domestic court nor at the Tribunal, and thus, of course, had to be dealt with in much more detail to explain to him the procedure of the court and to allay any fears he might have and to make him feel comfortable with giving testimony. I can tell you that yesterday we met beginning at 4.00 and we had to cut the proofing short after the witness indicated he was tired and he wished to go back to the hotel. We have instructions from VWS to always keep in mind the witness and not to overtax them, and that is what we were relying upon yesterday. That is, I believe, what I can present to you as additional information. We -- I -- I believe that there were additional matters that I wanted to raise with him in proofing that I did not raise, but I leave it upon Your Honours to make a decision as to whether -- as to how we will proceed, and we will abide by any decision you make. Thank you.
