utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, how long did you meet with the witness yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From 4.00 until just before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness had had the whole of that day -- he was not -- there was no interference in his programme by the Defence team, so that means that until 4.00 there were no specific matters he should look after?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Unless he had matters with VWS. VWS sometimes has a schedule of their own that I'm not privy to, but as Your Honours know, I was in court until 2.15 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just briefly consult with my colleagues. And you said and this morning you resumed your conversations with the witness at what time, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I met him at the hotel at 9.00. At approximately 9.15, 9.20 we arrived back at my apartment office to work, and then we started working until approximately 10.30, when word came to me that he might be required to testify this morning, and then I sent the proofing statement which was just rather briefly typed in an e-mail because I wanted to comply with all the instructions that I'd been given. And I point out that the changes in reductions in the cross time by the Prosecution, basically, prior to those, this witness was scheduled to begin on Monday, which is why the scheduling was done the way that it was done to have -- we considered we'd have sufficient time, even for a new witness, to proof him during that time-period that we thought we were going to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it from your brief note that at least you went to and through paragraph 12 of the witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this statement is 14 pages. Let me just look --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 14 paragraphs, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14 paragraphs, yes. Let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where earlier said that we -- that we had an early finish yesterday, I was mistaken because it was the day before yesterday, so I apologise for that. The Chamber has considered the situation and is of the opinion that the witness should have been ready. Even if you give sufficient time for a witness to rest, that doesn't mean that you start at 4.00 where you could have started at 2.30 or 3.00. Apart from that, the statement is extremely short. Apart from that, paragraphs 13 and 14, well, contain not that much that you would need to consider whether the witness should in any way reconsider that because it's mainly what he doesn't know. I mean, that wouldn't change that much during proofing, I take it, or at least it should not take that much time. Nevertheless, the Chamber is not forcing at this moment the Defence to bring this witness this morning, but adds to it a very strong warning that this should not happen again, and that next time we think we would be fully justified to force you under similar circumstances, but we refrain from doing it now. And the Defence should always be prepared to organise its preparations in such a way that there would be a reserve witness ready, which is, as was shown over the many, many years in this Tribunal, is well possible within the time limits of arrival and departure of a witness which the Victims and Witness Section accepts as normal. Let that be clear. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to thank Your Honours for understanding our position, and I can assure you that we will adjust our schedule of arriving future witnesses based on such situations, so we'll have to have more witnesses ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and whether you should change your schedule, Mr. Lukic, if that brings you into conflict with VWS, then it could also be that you would use your time better once the witness has arrived. So I leave that in your hands, whether the one is the reasonable solution or whether the other is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to add, I've just been told by our support staff, it was something I should have known, the time that the witnesses are permitted to stay or anticipated to stay per VWS has been shortened due to the number of witnesses that stayed for prolonged periods at the beginning of the case when the -- their testimony lasted longer than was the estimates. So we do have some limitations in terms of how long a witness can arrive prior to their scheduled testimony and how long they can stay. We also had instances where witnesses were staying longer than originally anticipated by VWS were sent back to their country of origin because of the financial restraints of keeping them here longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it seems that you do not understand what I said earlier. I was not discussing the policy. I wondered why you had not started yesterday at 2.30, why you had you not started at 3.00. Why two hours a day is too much of a burden for a witness and that he is tired instead of saying, Well, another half an hour or we should have started half an hour earlier. And that knowing that you have no other witnesses, that you should have completed the job, urging the witness how important it was, and saying that instead of two hours, that you could have asked him to spend three hours on a day which leaves, on a normal working day, five hours of additional rest. That is our primary concern, not your conversations with the Victims and Witness Section. Let's proceed and let the present witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the usher is getting the witness, I know that I'll be asking to look at Exhibit D582, if that saves some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the break took a little bit longer than expected. We had to deal with a procedural matter. Ms. MacGregor will now continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you'll see on the screen in front of you is the document that Mr. Stojanovic asked you about earlier. Now, you testified that you saw the original of this document. How did you -- in what circumstance did you see the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is fact that I have seen the original of this document. This was - I'm not sure about the exact date, but approximately a month after the conflicts broke out - in the office of Josip Milicevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Filipovic"], the president of the municipality of Foca, at his invitation, and he invited me over for coffee so that we could discuss the situation and the actual beginning of the war. And I took advantage of the situation or the opportunity to talk about the situation which he was in at that time. We were in practically the same situation but I was -- I participated from the very beginning of the armed conflict, and he was with other people and he was actually involved in a meeting, and the outcome of that meeting was this agreement. On the basis of our talk, he showed me this document on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You describe being in the same situation as Mr. Milincic [sic], what do you mean -- or excuse me, Filipovic. Although I'm not sure if the transcript recorded the name correctly. Can you repeat the name of who you were meeting with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Josip Milicevic, the president of Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. You described being in the same situation as him, the same situation that he was being in at the time. What do you -- what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I said that we were in different positions, I clarified a while ago where I was on the 8th of April, and he was in the municipal building at the same time when the conflict began. I am referring to the morning of the 8th of April, 1992. Mr. Milicevic, together with the other persons whom I already mentioned, members of the Executive Committee, was conducting talks and negotiations on the situation in Foca. The upshot, the outcome of their talks is this document which is in front of me, this agreement, this two-page agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So to be closure, that's a meeting that occurred on August -- excuse me, April 8th, that you were not present at?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I never said that I was present to the talks and the signing of this agreement. I said that I saw this document about a month later, when, on one occasion when talking to the president of Foca municipality, we discussed that event because I had found out from my brother via radio that the meeting was ongoing and that for that reason we were not to open fire without any specific orders. And that was interesting for me, and as he saw my position and my view of matters interesting on that day, the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask for clarification, Madam Prosecutor. I'm trying to follow your story, sir, Mr. Nikolic, earlier you were asked by Judge Fluegge who signed the document and instead you told us of people who were present at the time. Now you're saying you didn't attend this meeting. How did you know the people who were present if you were not in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signatures are affixed to the original document of all these people that I mentioned, and also Josip Milicevic also mentioned all those who had been present in our talk. And all who had been present also signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, what is the relationship between you and the president of Foca municipality that he would want to ask you to have a coffee with him? Was that a close relationship that you had?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We were on exceptionally friendly terms, and for a long time prior to the war we were exceptionally good friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before this disappears from the screen, I would like to ask a question in relation to paragraph 16 of this document. I read there: "The return of captured prison inmates to the Foca KP Dom." Mr. Nikolic, have you any idea what that could mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what it means. In that period, I do not know how, and under what circumstances, and at whose orders, but it was a fact that all the prisoners who were serving their regular sentences, so not prisoners of war, but all prisoners who happened to be at that time in the KP Dom were released, whether Serbs or Muslims or of any other ethnicity. Somebody had released them all. This caused fear and sowed panic among the population, irrespective of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 10, last sentence, you say: "That is when they withdrew from the KP Dom, having previously released all the inmates, both Muslim and Serb." When did this release happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I kindly ask for this statement to be shown me on the screen for me to be able to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is D581. It must be page 3, paragraph 10. It's now on the screen in B/C/S. Please have a look at the last sentence of paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So talking about this last part of the sentence, which says "and before that, all prisoners, both Muslims and Serbs, who had been released from the prison," that refers precisely to what I was saying before. The regular prisoners, practically all prisoners who had been sentenced by final judgement in the prewar state were there, and that is whom I mean. Although, I do not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- I'm asking you when they were released. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know the exact date, but I believe that it was a day before the conflict began. I believe it was a day or two or, rather, day before, but I do not have exact information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, you are describing Muslims leaving Foca town out of fear. Was that before the conflict, the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have interpretation. Nobody managed to translate your words for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'll repeat. In paragraph 10, you are describing Muslims leaving Foca town out of fear. Was that before the conflict, the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to explain to you the atmosphere and the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, please. I'm only focusing on the time. When did the Muslim people leave? When were these people from KP Dom released? I'm just asking you for a time-frame. When did all that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority of the Muslims, armed people and inhabitants, left in the night between the 12th -- on the night of the 12th, actually. And the prisoners, the convicts, better to put it, had been released before that. Not during the conflict. Or as a consequence of -- not as people who were imprisoned as a consequence of the war conflict. When I said this in my statement, I was referring to people who were serving regular prison sentences. Although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I have information that the Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I fully understand that. I just wanted to know the sequence. Now I understand what you were saying by "having previously released all the inmates." I understood at first it was on the first day, but now you are explaining that happened quite a while before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have still a few questions on this matter. What's the source of your knowledge of this, of the prisoners being released? Were you there when it happened? How did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I left the initial position and when we got to the village of Prevrac, where my family was, the entire population was panic stricken because they had received information that armed convicts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. I want to know what is the source of your information about the release of the prisoners. Did you learn that when it happened? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at the time when it happened, but rather a few days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question then is: When exactly was it that you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was the 9th, the night between the 9th and the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier started an answer, "rather a few days," and I expected you to say a few days after it had happened. Could you now tell us then in more detail when exactly those convicts were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be more precise than I've already been, because I did not have any timely information; that is to say, I have provided the source as to when and how I found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how did you know that both Serb convicts and Muslim convicts were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment I did not know, but when it says that they were all released, then I imagine it's one and the other and the third, if you will. All ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, one second, please. You say "when it says that they all were released," I read that as your statement, but from your answer I do understand that you do not really know whether both Muslim and Serb prisoners were released because you say "I imagine," which means not knowledge but rather a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. However, if you allow me, I received the exact information from the warden of the KP Dom who, at the time when I took part in government, held the office of the president of the Executive Board. I spoke to him about that in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, who was the warden of the KP Dom when these prisoners were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he was of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were you ever able to verify whether Muslim convicts had been released in reality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By talking to Mr. Tesovic who explained the situation to me, I mean the one that prevailed at that moment, because as I've already said, he was the warden of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what he told you, but whether it happened or not you were unable to verify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There was no need for me to verify. That was not a subject that I was interested in. I just meant in terms of my personal needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now did he also explain why he released all those convicts which then caused such panic among the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know Mr. Tesovic. I have known him for many years. I knew him before the war as well. He was a highly moral and responsible individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His assessment was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the morality of Mr. Tesovic. I'm asking you whether he explained why he had released all those convicts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I wanted to say. I had just prefaced it with something else. His personal assessment and his responsibility was such, and his conclusion was that he could not provide for the security and safety of those prisoners, and that is why he released all of these persons. According to my information, according to what I learned from him -- as a matter of fact, even part of the prisoners who had committed some serious crimes, he tried to organise their transfer to some other prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand you well that it was Mr. Tesovic, his decision, to release those prisoners, being the warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this conversation and the information that he provided to me, I am speaking to you. That is the information that I am conveying to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Tesovic remain to be the warden at -- on from the moment that these convicts were released, did he remain to be the warden of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He had certain problems because of these steps he had taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I take you back to your statement and go to the second part of paragraph 10. You said: "I learned later that many Muslim civilians had left Foca with their armed forces in the course of the night." And I continue: "They did it out of fear and no proclamation or order was issued to that effect by the Serbian military or civilian authorities." Where you say "they did it out of fear," did you refer to the Muslim civilians leaving Foca with their armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I continue to read, where it says: "That is when they withdrew from the KP Dom, having previously released all the inmates, both Muslim and Serb." Who are "they" in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not saying that they were released. I mean, that they released the Muslims. Well, before that -- I mean, this is a statement; namely, that all prisoners - Muslims and Serbs, that is -- please, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I stop you there. I read the beginning of this sentence: "That is when they withdrew from the KP Dom ..." Who withdrew from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslim armed forces under the control of the Muslim Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where it reads: "That is when they," that is, the Muslim forces, "withdrew from the KP Dom, having previously released all the inmates, both Muslims and Serb," that suggests - the language seems to be clear - that the Muslims had released them and you just told us that it was the Serb warden that had released them. Have you -- do you have an explanation for this, what seems to be a contradiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right when you say that this is not worded properly. There were two parties to this war, to this conflict, and there are no joint prisoners. Therefore, as for the meaning of this sentence, this is what I'm stating and this is my interpretation. It is badly worded. It would have been better had they said "convicts" before that, because I never mentioned that before and I thought that that was an important thing. And it was important that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You have reviewed this statement and you've signed it. Did you at that moment see that the wording was not what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I know that it is hard to translate the statement from Serbian into English, French, et cetera, but for me there is no dilemma. There is nothing unclear here. I read this in Serbian and I'm speaking Serbian. I believe that this formulation is puzzling for you but it's not for me. I'm adding this explanation in terms of the situation involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's wrongly translated, we'll have that verified. We'll look at it again and we'll ask our interpreters, and some of the members of the Defence team are bilingual, they can read both the one and the other, and if you say it's a translation issue, then we'll verify that. It brings me to another question, which is the following: You were interviewed on the 8th of March, if I see correctly. Was your statement put on paper on that same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That statement and conversation, I mean the one that was drafted on the occasion of the first conversation. I didn't want to sign that statement at first because it was a note. I mean, the Defence insisted that I sign this. I didn't want to until I saw the complete statement. And it is only then that I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say a first statement was made on the day when you were interviewed, although you didn't sign it. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct. During the first interview I did not sign a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why were you hesitant or reluctant to sign that if it reflected what you had said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a technical point of view, it had not been completed. They did not have the technical conditions for writing the proper statement, like the one that was compiled during the second meeting. You notice that there were no technical errors. There were different mistakes, though, in terms of names. So I insisted that the text be clear, that it be e-mailed to me, and then I signed that statement. That is why I insisted. I think that this really matters. And this may have seemed a bit confusing during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You received it by e-mail when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a few days -- a few days now -- oh, please, within a few days, I cannot say exactly, I got the e-mail. I have that noted down, of course, when I received the e-mail and when I returned it. I had to scan the statement, then I had to sign the statement, and then return the statement by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you did? You signed it and you returned it. How did you return it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] E-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think you also told us that you signed it in Foca during a meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. During the meeting I did not sign it. I mean, during the interview. A statement was drafted with quite a few mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You received the statement through e-mail. You signed it. You returned it. Were there any mistakes in that statement that you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there weren't any, as far as I could notice. I didn't find any mistakes, except for that poor wording that you objected to a moment ago. But I did not react because it was understandable to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why did you then have to go, if I understand you well, on the 8th of June to, if I understand you well, again sign the statement? You told us that you arrived late, you did see some others, they had a conversation but you did not know what about. You told us all that. Was that -- was that on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I met on two occasions with a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. The first meeting was in a catering establishment a month or two before. They then insisted that I should come for a talk and that was the first talk. It was then that between the two -- between two obligations that I had, I took advantage of the opportunity to meet with Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Dundjer, and I do not remember who else was there. At that time present were some people, and I did not pay any attention to them. I didn't even have the time for that. I mentioned some names that I could recall. It was only after a month or two, I cannot be precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. The statement says that you were interviewed on the 8th of March and that you signed on the 8th of June. That makes two occasions. Are you telling us that on the 8th of March, that you had a conversation and that Mr. Stojanovic was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what do you do you mean by "believe"? Was he there or wasn't he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is the date, the one that you are mentioning. I know that there were two interviews. The first interview -- at the first interview were present Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Dundjer. At the second interview, only Mr. Dundjer was present and another person whose name I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And that were the two only occasions when you met with the Mladic Defence; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you told us that a statement was sent to you by e-mail, that you signed it, and that you returned it. You also told us that a statement was given to you for signature but you said: I don't want to sign it because I want to see the complete statement. Now, I take you back to the two occasions when you met. That incomplete statement, Mr. Nikolic, was that given to you at the end of the first meeting you had where Mr. Stojanovic was present, or was it at the end of the second meeting you had where you said Mr. Dundjer was there with another person but not Mr. Stojanovic. Was it at the end of the first or at the end of the second meeting that you refused to sign an incomplete statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the first meeting, I gave absolutely no statements, nor were any minutes kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So was it then after the second meeting that you were given a -- offered to sign a statement which you were reluctant to do and finally did not do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. The statement which was offered to me to sign, first of all, was full of grammatical mistakes and the village names were wrong, for instance, that of the village of Prevrac. I cannot remember what was in it. So I insisted on that. And they jotted down my suggestions and they edited the statement in that sense. But I believe that it was also the result of the fact that the Defence team was in a hurry. So in order not to lose time, we agreed that they would send me the revised statement via e-mail and that I would sign it and return it to them in the same way, which I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still have those e-mails; that is, the statement that was sent to you? And do you have a copy --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you also have a copy of the first incomplete statement which you were reluctant to sign and did not sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not. I see no point in keeping something that I didn't sign as a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now on a further detail. You said the first meeting, it was not a real interview. It was only the second time, they were in a hurry. Was this statement prepared already when you had this second meeting with them, where you said you didn't want to sign because it was an incomplete statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The outcome of our talks and of the giving of my statement was the drawing up of the statement which I was supposed to sign, but after I had read it, I noticed that, as I've just said a while ago, what I noticed, and I gave you the reasons why I wouldn't sign it until all those shortcomings were removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that second meeting, how long lasted that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least half an hour. I cannot be precise. I didn't keep time. But certainly not under half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I can guarantee. But I cannot say with precision how long it took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But was it, to see what maximum time it would have taken, was it more than one hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. Possibly. Sometimes when time is filled with substance, like, for instance, with talk, like today, I'm really surprised to see how much time has already passed. That might happen. So I cannot say with precision, but it is possible that it lasted over an hour, in fact. I'm not sure. And, of course, I wouldn't wish to give you some inaccurate information. I'm not sure about the duration of our interview, when it began and when it ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said they were in a hurry. Could you tell us what made you believe that they were in a hurry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Mr. Dundjer told me that he had more potential witnesses with whom he was to conduct interviews. After I had finished, I saw Mr. Radojica Mladjenovic in passing outside. I think that they had allotted precise slots in terms of time which would be devoted to these potential witnesses. As far as I recall, my scheduled time was at 9.00, but of course I didn't see any need for me to remember that particular time but I do think I -- it seems to me that it was 9.00. I was there on time. How much it lasted, I cannot say with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you think you saw another witness waiting who was scheduled for later that day? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see him before you entered the room where you had this conversation, or did you see when you left that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Namely, afterwards we were talking. We had these interviews in a -- in a room on the first floor. It was on my way out of the building that I came across Mr. Mladjenovic and I assumed that he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you remember that you finished before lunchtime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was certainly before lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what do you consider to be lunchtime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what regular lunchtime might be, p.m., of course. Breakfast is in the morning. Lunch is in the afternoon, and dinner - and I personally do not have dinner as a rule - but it's about 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's dinner time. But lunchtime is at 12.00 for you, at midday, or is it at 1.00 or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I usually have lunch after working hours. And my working hours end at half past 3.00 p.m., and I only have my lunch then. I use a break to have breakfast, if I may finish, and that break is from 10.00 to 10 -- to 10 past 10.00, and I might have a snack later if I'm hungry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break soon, don't worry. One issue remaining for me, which is: Was the name of Mr. Mandic mentioned at all? We see that it is in the English version, not in the version in your own language. But was the name of Mr. Mandic mentioned at all when you met with Mr. Dundjer and when you were interviewed? Did they ask about it or did you say something about -- even if you had said: I don't know him or -- was his name mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, so many names from the Defence team, and today also by the Prosecutor, that were mentioned. I do not rule out the possibility that the name of Mandic and that of Elez and Kunarac and Jankovic, that all these name were mentioned. I gave my statement in respect of the facts and circumstances that I was knowledgeable about. I do not rule out the possibility that in the interview we did mention Mandic. Concretely, I don't know which Mandic. The Mandics are a large family. I could not even -- I could not say yes or no. It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anyone by the name of Mandic who you considered to be in command of whatever unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, this is a large family, that of the Mandics. I know one Mandic who was the commander of a platoon and later of a company, even a neighbour of mine, whose first name I do not know, he is a neighbour of mine. And I know quite a few other members of the Mandic family. I don't know what their roles were or what their positions were during the war, so I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, do you have this e-mail in which you were sent the statement? Do you -- did you take that with you when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have it in The Hague, but I have it in my computer, in my e-mail. But, of course, I have a reservation there, I might have deleted it accidentally. But I'm convinced that this message is still in my e-mail folder, so if you need it, I can also send it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you're willing to provide it to the Chamber, that is the e-mail message and the attachment or the statement which was attached and which you signed and returned, that would be appreciated. Ms. MacGregor. Judge Fluegge has one question for you. I know that we have stolen quite a bit of your -- or at least it's not stolen because it's still your time, Ms. MacGregor, but we intervened for a quite long series of questions. I suggest that you continue after the break but give an opportunity to Judge Fluegge to put one question to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the Presiding Judge asked you about the second meeting with the Defence team, which started 9.00 in the morning. When did that take place? On which day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was nothing which would have prompted me to actually remember that date. I don't know what date it was. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking you because only one date is noted in your witness statement, date of interview 8 March 2014. This is only one interview, but you told us that two interviews were conducted -- or meetings, at least, with the Defence team. Was it, the second one, on the 8th of March or later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sequence of my encounters of my meetings is what I've just explained. The first encounter, the actual introductions, the meeting, and they're asking me the question whether I would be a Defence witness for General Mladic, and I accepted them. At that meeting we had no further discussions about any other subject, because I was in a hurry. They just would -- said that they would take my telephone number, call me, and schedule a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that only one substantial meeting took place, one interview with the content which we can find in the statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the result of this second meeting that you're referring to was the statement which I wouldn't sign, and I explained why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again, that first meeting took place where? In what city?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this second meeting was also in Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at two minutes to 2.00, but only after the witness has left the court -- 10 minutes to 2.00 but only after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, I hardly dare to ask you how much time you'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My estimate is 10 to 15 minutes. I fully expect to be finished before the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- of this session, with time for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that the time the Chamber has taken doesn't need much of an explanation. There is some concern about the taking of statements. Mr. Lukic, if suddenly names appear in the English version which do not appear in the B/C/S version, and if the witness explains to us that what we find in the English version is really not what he intended to say, then we have some concerns about the way in which statements are taken and that explains why the Chamber took more than usual to explore that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I -- I would suggest that he reads that sentence in B/C/S so it could be translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- maybe on the record to -- so at least to correct it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was -- is it a CLSS translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you know whether it's a CLSS translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That last question remains, for the time being, without an answer. And, Mr. Lukic, you know that interpreters are not in a way prepared for the interpretation so as to either correct or to change any written translation, which is, of course, prepared in a different way with the access to all kind of dictionaries and rethinking. So therefore, that's not a very good matter. Ms. MacGregor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in response to Mr. Stojanovic's questions you testified that from time to time you were engaged with the VRS during the war; for example, religious holidays and some incidents. Can you give an example of an incident where you would have been engaged by the VRS, other than the incident that you've described on Saint Nicholas Day at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, there was this offensive launched by the Muslim forces against the area of the municipality of Trnovo on Mount Treskavica. Or rather, our positions were on the very slopes of the mountain of Treskavica. The work platoon was there, the one that I belonged to, and it included about 120 soldiers. And they were busy there for about three months. That's an example because there was this Muslim army offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: A few things there. When you refer to the work platoon that you were part of, are you referring to your brother's unit that we have been talking about today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, that was a separate unit as a reserve of people who had the obligation to work during the war. That is why it is called work obligation or the unit consisting of persons like myself who were engaged for work assignments during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say that you were a member of the VRS reserves during the war and that periodically you would be called up to perform work obligation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way, too. So from the moment when in the territory of the municipality of Foca, as an organisational part of the Army of Republika Srpska, the forces of the TO, until then, and other units that I assume were parts of the Territorial Defence, they became part of the Army of Republika Srpska, became an integral part of it. As far as I can remember, the period involved is either the beginning of July, if I remember correctly, or the very end of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: From July onward, your role was as a reserve member of that unit that you've just -- of this entity, the VRS, even though it wasn't always the VRS; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I think from around the 18th of June or on the basis of the decision of the president of the Executive Board, I was sent for work obligation. From then onwards, all the way up until that incident that took place on Saint Nicholas Day that I spoke about, I had not been involved anywhere. Rather, I had work obligation. And then, I've already explain this, when Major Pejovic called, during that incident, during that case I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, please listen to what I'm saying. You've stated that you did not have a formal role in the VRS, but you've described now two situations, at least, where you were near or in fighting circumstances involving VRS forces. All I'm trying to understand is why, if you were not in any way a formal member of the VRS, you would be called periodically to report to a front line situation and what you did at the front line situation. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, all of us, most of us, were an organised, disciplined organisation that knew what it was doing. I've explained my status when I was part of the Territorial Defence. Later on I had work obligation. When military organisation was introduced in respect of the Army of Republika Srpska, then, when necessary, people were engaged in work obligation status, and then I was called up when necessary. I think I'm saying this clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: How would you receive the information that you'd been called up? What was the method that you would be contacted by?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Written call-up papers. They were brought to my place of work by soldiers. These were mobilisation call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Would you wear a uniform when you showed up for duty?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the one that I had available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Which was what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, after those clashes in town, the unit commanded by my brother gave me a military uniform, camouflage, as a token of appreciation. This was a donation. It came in from I don't know where, but I always wore that when I took part in armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did it have a VRS insignia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I personally did not wear VRS insignia. There was this emblem that I had on the sleeve --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Depending on the situation, we would wear ribbons too, in order to recognise one another in certain situations. These were specific things so that we could recognise each other. Most soldiers had these emblems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Switching subjects. After June 18th, 1992, did you continue to see members of your late brother's unit in Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: At this point was the unit commanded by a man named Brane Cosovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That unit was commanded by Brane Cosovic, not Kosovic. It is a "ch."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. But the unit still was referred to as the Dragan Nikolic Unit in honour of your brother; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The exact name was the anti-sabotage -- well, if this is going to be correct, what I'm going to utter now, that is what I know, the Anti-Sabotage Detachment Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We've talked about the Gojko Jankovic unit and the Kunarac unit. Did you spend time with those units in Foca during 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a house located in Trnovace that Gojko Jankovic would sometimes use and go to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. To this day I don't know which house is Mr. Jankovic's. I know that it is in Trnovace, but as for this exact location and house, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard evidence that a house in Trnovace was used by Mr. Jankovic and Kunarac to imprison and rape Muslim girls after Foca fell to the Serbs. Do you -- have you ever heard of such a thing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have heard but I heard of that only after the war, after these people had been put on trial, prosecuted. But during the war, I never heard any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And from your answer, I take it you're aware that Mr. Kunarac and others were convicted here by this Tribunal in 2001? I see you're nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the judgement in that case, the Trial Chamber stated that Mr. Kunarac and his associates frequently used the house in Trnovace for the rape of Muslim girls. In that same judgement -- and right now I'm referring to a judgement from a Trial Chamber, not this Trial Chamber, but in the Kunarac case. In that same judgement at paragraph 269, the Chamber states Witness FWS-191 -- and that's a pseudonym referring to a witness in that case. This witness was also raped by: "... another soldier called Zoran Nikolic. The latter raped her twice, once when 'Zaga' was in the house ..." And this paragraph refers to the time-period of August or September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record I'll refer the Defence and the Chamber to paragraph 269 of that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you aware that the judgement in a case here mentions your name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I am not familiar with the details. I would like you to tell me. Because in Foca also prior to the war there existed two -- at least two Zoran Nikolics, with an identical name and surname. I do know that in a group that I have talked about which came from Montenegro, there was a member of that group, there was a person by the name of Zoran Nikolic. If you have other information, please tell me the year of birth, the name of the father, and other particulars for the purpose of identification because we would not wish to mislead anyone that they might think that this actually concerns or relates to me. It would be fair in the very least.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: From your answer, I don't understand if there is two or three Zoran Nikolics. I see that there are two before the war, yourself, and another person, and then you mention a Zoran Nikolic from Montenegro. Is that, in fact, a third person or is that also a person who was there before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were two Zoran Nikolics who lived -- who were there and lived there before the war. A third Zoran Nikolic was a member of a group that had come from Montenegro, and I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. I'm with some concern looking at the clock, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is my last topic for questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your last topic. But, Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a couple of minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to know, perhaps, Madam Registrar, you could assist, whether we could extend for not more than five to ten minutes today's session because it's the last session of the week. Madam Registrar is quite confident that we'll be -- that all those assisting us would allow us to finish the evidence of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I only have one final question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, as you've heard, we're trying to finish, so I want to respond. I've reviewed the evidence underlying the judgement, and I don't have the information about the date of birth that you've asked for, so all I can ask you is: Is this Zoran Nikolic, who is being referred to in the chamber -- excuse me, in the judgement, is this a true accusation about yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, without a warning under Rule 90(E) you can't put this question to the witness. So either you invite me to do it or refrain from that question because the witness says it's unfair to relate it to him where there were others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I ask you to give the warning then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- so I can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this last question, Mr. Nikolic, I inform you about our Rules. Our Rules says: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." I would like to inform you that if you have concerns that by answering the question in accordance with the truth that you would incriminate yourself, that you may address me and ask to be relieved from answering that question. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you the soldier called Zoran Nikolic who in the Chamber's judgement in Kunarac raped twice a Muslim detainee at the house of Kunarac in Trnovace -- or Jankovic in Trnovace?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we see in e-court, I believe it's D581, paragraph 3. I think it is now in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to go to the first page -- or there is -- I think it's the second page, but at least to the page on which paragraph 3 appears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, in order to overcome this problem, because we have an incongruence between the English translation and B/C/S, I shall just ask you this: Talking about the second sentence here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference, please? The interpreter does not have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 on the screen, is that -- second sentence. Please put your question to the witness, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Was this unit that you said contained -- consisted of three platoons, does that have its separate command and commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was directly subordinated to the head of the Crisis Staff, as I've already said, because -- actually, I concluded that having been present at a talk and communication between my brother and the Crisis Staff. I cannot give you any further details because I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In -- was the commander, or the komandir, the commander of one of these three platoons someone who went by the last name of Mandic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The people I knew were my brother and Mr. Brane Cosovic. And as I've already said, I was not formally a member of that group and I actually have explained in which way I became a member of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I shall only ask you another thing in order for us to clarify the time of the taking of the statement. When you first met with the Defence team of General Mladic and when you also mentioned the name of Mr. Stojanovic, was any statement taken from you in the sense of a written text?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could that have been on the 17th of January, 2014?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I've said already ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I've said already -- I said a while ago that I could not remember the exact date because it meant nothing to me. I did not consider it of the essence, that particular date, on what date it was. I know that we conducted the interview and I know that there was an event that I attended, and I can tell you what it was. I was present at an interview which was conducted with a number of persons -- with many persons, over 300 persons were being interviewed on that day and I was there by virtue of the work that do. For that, I could hardly actually find the time to meet with you. I don't know exactly now what date it was, but taking that event as a reference, I could subsequently inform you of the exact date of our interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I should conclude with this question: When asked by the Defence team of General Mladic then, specifically myself, did you promise that you would be prepared to conduct an interview with the Defence team about what you knew about events in Foca in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, thank you. That concludes my questioning. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. I have a few very short questions, and I would like to ask you to respond to them in a very brief way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of arming and distribution of weapons among the Serbs in 1991 and 1992 in Foca? And I'm thinking in terms of hundreds and thousands. Do you have any personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge for 1991. Or I do have some knowledge but not about -- in terms of hundreds of thousands, the quantities that you referred to. As I said before, my platoon was involved in the procurement, transport, and distribution of weapons. These were not quantities that could be measured in terms of some huge numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there immediately. I was thinking in a time-frame well before the war started.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: Do you have any personal knowledge about Muslim prisoners in KP Dom, prisoners of war, their treatment, and what happened to them? I'm asking you again for any personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I never set foot in the KP Dom or the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no personal knowledge, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was just about to say except that, as I've already said, that my parents lived in the direction of Miljevina, 10 kilometres away from Foca. Because of the crisis and the lack of fuel - I had my own car but I had no fuel - I was compelled when I went there to stop -- to hitch-hike, sorry. At a certain point, the van from the KP Dom arrived and they stopped for me and they told me that there was -- I could not sit next to the driver but I could only sit in the rear, the section which is used for other purposes. I didn't actually pay any attention and didn't know what lay in store, and I entered the rear of the van in which there were Muslim prisoners who were being taken to work in the Miljevina mine there. I recognised some people. I was surprised, I have to say, unpleasantly. At the first moment they asked me whether I had any cigarettes. I did. I gave them cigarettes, and then I asked them, concretely, the brother -- about the brother of one of those men, where he was, and he said that his brother was in the KP Dom. Then I disembarked the van near the house where my parents lived, and I decided to go and visit this friend of mine because he was a colleague from work. I asked them whether they needed anything, and they said that they needed nothing but cigarettes, and that they had food which was very good and which was better than otherwise because of the work that they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you have no personal knowledge about the food, how it was prepared. That's hearsay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I heard that directly from a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I mean by hearsay. I have no further questions. Have my questions triggered any need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I do have one follow-up question. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Based on your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you remember, approximately, the date of the incident where you were in the van with the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please don't make me go back all that way. After all, it's been 20 years, if not even more than that. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know, tell us. If you say you don't remember the date, then that's an answer as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Could it have been in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No way. It was either 1993, middle of the year, or the end of 1993. Please don't take my word for the exact date, but there is no way it could have been October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony. Witness, I would like to ask your co-operation. Earlier we -- Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what happened to the man that you talked to and what happened to his brother that he said was at the KP Dom Foca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Both of these men that I did not mention by name, specifically, were exchanged at a given point in time. To the best of my knowledge, I know for sure for one of them, because he visited me after the war, he came to see me, and he even brought me gifts, I know that he is alive. And he had been a prisoner, I think, for almost two years at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ekrem Cemo, that colleague of mine. He was my colleague from work and a friend. A colleague from work and a friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about the fate of his brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me that he was alive and that he had been exchanged as well. Now further on, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then no further questions triggered by questions by the Bench. Witness, I would like to seek your co-operation. If you could have access to your e-mail account through the internet, which is usually possible, would you be willing, if assisted by technical staff of the Tribunal, to see whether you can retrieve already right away this afternoon your e-mail exchange in relation to your statement, are you willing to explore that possibility with the assistance of our technicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would fail to retrieve the e-mail through that means, then of course we would like to invite you then to send it from where you live to the Victims and Witness Section. And since we do not know what will appear from those messages, we cannot exclude for certain that there would be any need for a recall. And under those circumstances, both parties are hereby instructed not to contact the witness, and you should not be in contact with anyone about your testimony, especially not the parties, up till the moment once you have retrieved your e-mails. Then, of course, you are free again -- yes, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If there is any way to allow a bit time between when he's retrieved the e-mail and any response from the Prosecution should the Prosecution also -- if the Chamber chooses to review the e-mail, just in case we do choose to recall him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say then -- okay. Until further order, Witness, you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, the testimony you have given, and I'm not saying how likely it is but we cannot exclude for the full hundred per cent that you would be recalled. And we would like to receive copy, through the Victims and Witness Section, of your e-mail exchange about your statement. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since it is likely that we might not see each other again, I would like to thank you already now for coming to The Hague and for the having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You may follow the usher. And please keep in touch with the Victims and Witness Section about the exercise to retrieve that e-mail, those e-mail exchanges. And, Madam Registrar, I take it that it has been clear enough until now what kind of assistance the Chamber expects both VWS and the technical staff to provide, and could you take care that that assistance is provided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would again like to thank -- give full thanks to -- yes. I first would like to thank all the interpreters, security, whoever allowed us to finish to conclude the testimony of this witness today, for their flexibility, and it's really highly appreciated. Then before we adjourn, I'd like to use this opportunity to inform the parties that the Chamber will deliver guidance before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I had done that already. Yes. Due to the revised witness schedule, Witness Milan Pejic, GRM206, is scheduled to testify as the third witness next week. Taking into account that the Defence corrigendum tendering the witness statement was filed on the 4th of July of this year, the time agreed upon between the parties regarding the calling of 92 ter witnesses will be undercut by a few days, and the Chamber would like to know what the parties' position is on the matter. At the same time, I think this could be exchanged -- unless you could do it in one or two words, Ms. Bibles, otherwise we do it through informal exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We're prepared to cross-examine that witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's hereby on the record. We adjourn and will resume Monday, the 21st of July, 2014, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
